sources.title: Top 5 loại cát trắng trải nền bể cá, hồ thủy sinh phổ biến
Cát bể cá là cát gì?
Cát Thạch Anh Màu Trắng Ngà Hạt To | Đá Thủy Sinh Vạn Xuân
Cát Nắng Vàng, Cát Trắng, Cát Thạch Anh Dùng Trải Nền, Trang Trí Bể Cá Thủy Sinh (bao 1Kg) - ShopCa

facts.fact: Name for the term: "Cát bể cá"
Name for the term: "cát trơ"
Sand under an aquarium can help biological filtration because nitrifying bacteria build up in it over time.
Fish often seem more settled over a sand bottom.
Corydoras catfish sift through sand for food, which helps keep it clean.
Coarse sands do some biological filtration, but less than gravel does.
Inert sand (cát trơ) holds no nutrients, so on its own it only suits plants that need no substrate fertiliser. Plants that feed from the substrate need a fertiliser layer underneath.
Sand laid over a substrate fertiliser layer supports plant roots, the nitrogen cycle, the breakdown of waste and beneficial microbes.
Play sand has grains of 0.004–0.018 in. It is poorly sieved, has many fines under 0.004 in, and can cloud water for months.
Pool filter sand has grains of 0.018–0.022 in. It is well sieved and washed and does not pack down easily.
Aquarium sand typically has grains of 0.04–0.06 in. It is closely sieved, with few fines.
Anaerobic sand shows as dark patches under stones and ornaments, and disturbing them releases a rotten-egg smell.
"Cát thạch anh trắng": the grains are round and even, with purity the shop gives as up to 99%, and they reflect light well.
"Cát thạch anh trắng" is chemically inert and does not raise pH or gH.
"Cát thạch anh trắng" is so bright that waste shows clearly if the bed is not vacuumed regularly.
"Cát thạch anh" is white, translucent and shiny, and comes mainly from the USA and the Netherlands.
"Cát thạch anh" is treated and cleaned before packing and can be used without further processing.
"Cát Thạch Anh Màu Trắng Ngà Hạt To" is an ivory-white quartz sand from Vietnam, with grains larger than sea sand.
"Cát Thạch Anh Màu Trắng Ngà Hạt To": rinse it thoroughly 3 to 5 times, as you would rinse rice, to remove dust. Then add water and let it settle until the water is clear.
"Cát nắng vàng" is a blend of off-white and pale yellow grains that looks like a natural streambed. It hides debris well.
"cát nắng vàng", "cát trắng" and "cát thạch anh" are sold as fine-grained substrate sands of Vietnamese origin in 1 kg bags.
"Cát muối tiêu" is a mix of white and very small black grains. It hides waste and early algae.
"Cát muối tiêu" does not raise pH and changes it only slightly. It sparkles under aquarium lights.
"Cát thạch anh siêu mịn" has powder-like grains of about 0.1–0.3 mm.
"Cát thạch anh siêu mịn" is very light. Strong filter flow can blow it into a cloud, or pull it into the filter and jam the impeller.
"Cát sông" is a natural sand of mixed minerals. It has no smell and is said not to affect water quality.
"Cát sông" suits soft-water fish such as tetras and cá chuột (Corydoras).
"Cát trắng" comes from the sea. It stains easily, so the tank needs cleaning more often.
"Cát san hô" is made from natural coral. It adds hardness and alkalinity, so it suits saltwater tanks, hard water and African cichlids.
Sand containing coral or shell can raise the water's hardness.
To wash sand, stir it in a bucket and pour off the cloudy water. Repeat 5–7 times until the water stays clear.
Natural river sand can be soaked in dilute potassium permanganate (KMnO4) for about 30 minutes, or boiled for 15 minutes.
When filling, pour the water onto a plastic sheet or a sponge so the sand bed is not disturbed.
Amount of sand: length × width × desired depth ÷ 1000 × 1.5 = kg of sand. For example, a 3 cm layer in a 60×40 cm tank takes about 10.8 kg.
Inert sand is spread directly in the tank to a depth of about 3–5 cm.
Rinse new inert substrates in tap water, agitating them until the water runs clear.
Rinse all sand well before it goes into the tank.
Add sand after the tank has cycled: the biofilm formed during cycling traps many of the fines.
Vacuum the sand bed regularly to remove dead organic matter. Coarser sands are much easier to vacuum.
Running your fingers through the sand loosens detritus and keeps it aerated, but a gravel vacuum is preferred.
Grey, tan or brown sand shows fish waste less than white sand, on which feces collect as visible brown mulm.
In marine tanks a sand layer of 1–3 cm is about right. Deep sand makes anaerobic problems worse.
Beach or playpit sand is unsuitable: it contains silicates that cause algae.
Construction sand often contains lime, which raises pH and hardness and clouds the water.
Sand sold as a building material may contain harmful impurities.
Fine sand laid over coarse gravel works its way down through it, and digging fish mix the layers.
Sand wears out pumps. A magnetic pump may last 6–12 months with sand, against 4–8 years with aquarium gravel.
Coarser sand from reputable brands has far fewer fines and only slightly shortens pump life.
Calcareous sand suits Rift Lake cichlids and hard-water fish such as mollies, but not most freshwater fish.
Aquarium Science calls it a myth that deep sand beds go anoxic and release hydrogen sulfide. In the author's year-long test of four 5-inch sand beds, none produced hydrogen sulfide.
Aquarium Science says sulfur-smelling bubbles from the substrate are mostly carbon dioxide with parts-per-billion H2S, which suggests low oxygen, probably from overfeeding.
In contrast, Swell UK says sand can turn anaerobic, and that anaerobic substrates harm rooted plants.
Aquarium Science calls it a myth that Black Diamond blasting sand wears away catfish barbels. It blames barbel erosion on high bacterial counts in mulm.
